lead: A flow can be named in four independent ways. Does the velocity at a fixed point change with time? Does it change from place to place? Is the motion orderly or randomly mixed? How many space coordinates does the velocity depend on? Each question has a plain test, and the answers combine freely. Engineers use these names to pick the right formula: a steady-flow energy equation for a nozzle, a uniform-flow assumption for a long pipe, a laminar formula for oil in a narrow tube.
prereq: You need the Eulerian velocity field from Chapter 2.1, so that V is known as a function of position and time.

blocks.text: The first naming question is about time only. A flow is steady at a point when the velocity there does not change with time, and unsteady when it does.

blocks.where: V is the velocity vector at a fixed point, in m/s; t is time, in s; ∂/∂t is the partial derivative with position (x, y, z) held constant.

items: Mark one fixed point in the flow field.
Measure or compute V at that point at several instants.
If V is the same every time, the flow is steady at that point.
Repeat elsewhere. The flow is steady only if the test passes everywhere.

blocks.text: A tap opened and left alone gives steady flow: the velocity at the tap mouth stays the same all morning. A pump trip during a Chennai power cut makes the velocity at each fixed point fall with time, so that flow is unsteady. A monsoon river is unsteady; a pipeline carrying a fixed discharge is steady.

Steady does not mean zero acceleration. A particle can speed up by moving to a place where the velocity is higher, even when nothing changes with time. That is the convective acceleration of Chapter 2.4.
The second question is about place. A flow is uniform when the velocity does not change from point to point along the flow direction at a given instant.

blocks.where: s is distance measured along the flow direction, in m; V is the velocity at that instant, in m/s.

blocks.text: In a long straight pipe of constant diameter the average velocity is the same at every section, so the flow is uniform. In a nozzle the area shrinks and the velocity rises from section to section, so the flow is non-uniform. A widening channel is non-uniform because its depth sets the area.

blocks.text: The two questions are independent, so steady non-uniform flow is common in machines.

The third question is about order. In laminar flow the fluid moves in thin layers that slide over each other and never mix. A dye thread injected into the stream stays a single clean thread far downstream. Honey poured from a spoon behaves this way.

In turbulent flow the motion is randomly mixed. Eddies form and break, particles cross between layers, and the velocity at a fixed point fluctuates about a mean. Fast smoke from a lamp, or water from a fully open tap, shows this.

items: Laminar: ordered layers, no cross-mixing, quiet, dye thread intact.
Turbulent: random eddies, strong mixing, hissing, dye thread destroyed.
Which appears depends on speed, pipe size and viscosity together, through the Reynolds number. That number and the changeover belong to Unit 4, Viscous Flow Through Pipes.

blocks.text: Laminar and steady are different ideas. A laminar flow can be unsteady, and a turbulent flow can be steady in the mean: the time-averaged velocity at a point stays constant even though it fluctuates.
The fourth question counts coordinates. A flow is one-dimensional when the velocity depends on one space coordinate only, two-dimensional for two, three-dimensional for three.

items: 1-D: average velocity along a pipe varies with distance along the axis only.
2-D: flow between long parallel plates, far from the side walls.
3-D: flow past a short bridge pier, or water entering a bell-mouth intake.

blocks.text: Compressible flow has density that changes with pressure; incompressible flow has constant density. Liquids such as water are treated as incompressible, and gases are incompressible at low speed. High-speed gas flow is covered in Unit 3, Fluid Dynamics and Flow Measurement.

A real fluid has viscosity and resists shear; an ideal fluid is a model with zero viscosity, used when friction is negligible. Unit 1, Fluid Properties and Fluid Statics, defines both. A flow is rotational if fluid elements spin about their own axes, and irrotational if they do not; Chapter 2.6 treats that properly.

Open channels use the same tests, adding gradually varied and rapidly varied as sub-classes of non-uniform flow. A surge or bore is rapidly varied and unsteady, as when a gate closes quickly on a canal.

figure.caption: Four independent questions decide the name of a flow, and one flow answers all four at once: a nozzle with a fixed discharge is steady, non-uniform, one-dimensional and laminar or turbulent depending on speed.

spec.aria: A tree with root Flow types and four branches: steady or unsteady judged by change with time, uniform or non-uniform by change with place, laminar or turbulent by order or mixing, and 1-D to 3-D by number of coordinates.

examples.question: Water flows at a steady 0.02 m³/s through a horizontal nozzle whose diameter falls from 100 mm at the inlet to 50 mm at the outlet. Find the area and mean velocity at each section. Then classify the flow with respect to time, place and number of coordinates.
steps: Area of a circle: A = πd²/4, with d in metres.
The same discharge passes both sections (continuity, Chapter 2.5): Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂.
Check: 0.007854 × 2.5465 = 0.02 m³/s and 0.0019635 × 10.1859 = 0.02 m³/s. Discharge is unchanged.
Time test: discharge is fixed, so at any fixed point the velocity does not change with time. The flow is steady.
Space test: velocity rises from 2.5465 m/s to 10.1859 m/s along the nozzle, so the flow is non-uniform.
Coordinate test: mean velocity depends on distance along the axis only, so the flow is one-dimensional.
examples.answer: A₁ = 0.007854 m², V₁ = 2.5465 m/s, A₂ = 0.0019635 m², V₂ = 10.1859 m/s; the flow is steady, non-uniform and one-dimensional.

import math
Q = 0.02
d1 = 0.100
d2 = 0.050
A1 = math.pi*d1**2/4
A2 = math.pi*d2**2/4
V1 = Q/A1
V2 = Q/A2
print(round(A1, 6))
print(round(V1, 4))
print(round(A2, 7))
print(round(V2, 4))

traps: Concluding that a non-uniform flow must be unsteady. The tests are independent: a nozzle with fixed discharge is steady and non-uniform.
Saying a steady flow has zero acceleration. Only ∂V/∂t is zero; the convective part remains, and in a nozzle it is large.
Treating uniform flow as meaning the velocity is identical everywhere in the field. It means no change along the flow direction at one instant, usually the cross-section average.
Mixing up laminar and steady. Laminar describes order of motion; steady describes constancy in time. A turbulent flow can be steady in the mean.
Forgetting that a slowly varying discharge, such as a pipe filling during pump start, is unsteady even when the velocity across the section is nearly uniform: unsteady uniform flow.

quiz.q: Define steady flow and write its condition in symbols.
quiz.a: A flow is steady if the velocity at every fixed point does not change with time. Condition: ∂V/∂t = 0 with position held constant.

quiz.q: Define uniform flow and say which coordinate the test uses.
quiz.a: A flow is uniform if the velocity does not change from point to point along the flow direction at a given instant: ∂V/∂s = 0, where s is distance along the flow.

quiz.q: A student says the flow in a nozzle cannot be steady because the velocity changes inside it. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Steadiness is tested at fixed points, not along the path. If discharge is constant, velocity at each fixed point is constant in time, so the flow is steady. The change from section to section is non-uniformity, a separate question.

quiz.q: Give one practical observation each that separates laminar from turbulent flow in a pipe.
quiz.a: Laminar: a dye thread stays a thin unbroken line, the flow is silent, no cross-mixing. Turbulent: the dye spreads and fills the pipe, the flow hisses, eddies and random fluctuations appear.

quiz.q: Water flows at 0.01 m³/s through a reducer from 80 mm diameter to 40 mm diameter. Find both mean velocities and classify the flow.
quiz.a: A₁ = π(0.08)²/4 = 0.0050265 m², V₁ = 0.01/0.0050265 = 1.9894 m/s. A₂ = π(0.04)²/4 = 0.0012566 m², V₂ = 0.01/0.0012566 = 7.9577 m/s. The flow is steady (fixed discharge) and non-uniform (velocity changes along the flow).

quiz.q: Can a flow be unsteady and still uniform? Give an example and justify it with the two tests.
quiz.a: Yes. Take a long constant-diameter pipe whose discharge is slowly increased by opening a valve. At one instant the cross-section average velocity is the same at every section, so ∂V/∂s = 0 and the flow is uniform in space. That same velocity rises with time at every fixed point, so ∂V/∂t ≠ 0 and the flow is unsteady. The two tests use different independent variables.

quiz.q: A canal receives a sudden surge when a gate opens upstream. Name the flow with all four labels and say which still apply far downstream one hour later.
quiz.a: The surge near the gate is unsteady, non-uniform, turbulent and three-dimensional, with 'rapidly varied' added as the open-channel description. One hour later, far downstream, the flow is close to steady, gradually varied and effectively one-dimensional; it is still non-uniform because depth changes along the canal, and turbulent in practice.

beyond: Not for the exam. Instruments answer the same four questions. A hot-wire or laser Doppler probe records velocity at a fixed point against time: a flat record means steady, fluctuations about a constant mean mean steady in the mean (as in turbulent flow), and a drift means unsteady. The randomness of the fluctuations, not their presence, marks turbulence. Particle image velocimetry maps whole planes at one instant and shows non-uniformity. A CFD solver is set to steady or unsteady before the mesh is built, and choosing wrongly wastes hours of computing.
